He then receives a letter reporting that two English ships have been lost by running aground in the Straits, three more nearly so, and a Dutch fleet has gone there, which he calls most sad news. Finally, he learns his canary bird of three or four years has died, which much troubles him.
canon.narrative.meaning: The naval losses are grave and the nation must be made sensible of their seriousness.

He also records the burial of his cousin Percivall Angier and the death of Dr. Tom Pepys, for whom he feels little sorrow, calling him a coxcomb and a shame to his family.

parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys visits Mr. Povy to resolve his trouble of mind about the Tangier treasurer position, offering it back on Povy's own terms, which Povy refuses. Creed then gives reasons from the auditors that Povy must be put back in, which Pepys finds hard to withstand, but also provides ingenious advice. Pepys procures an order for Povy's payment to himself, which if it passes will stop the thing from being fastened upon him. He dines with Creed, discovers Will Howe's dissembling, walks with Mr. Wren and Mr. Ager, and goes with his wife to Mile-End Greene. He receives alarming news of fleet engagement but then hears contrary reports that all is well, of which he is heartily glad.

Minnes noticed his frequent absence on non-office business. He was more troubled by his neglect in writing to Mr. Coventry, having even fallen asleep mid-letter and made many blots. The following day he made up his monthly accounts and found with great joy that he had gained above £100 clear that month, being worth above £1400, the greatest sum he had ever been worth. He dined with Mr. Spong, whom he greatly admired for modesty and ingenuity, and ended the month in great content as to his estate but in much trouble about Tangier business, with fears of sickness in the City.
parsed.narrative.meaning: He resolves to mind his business better and values himself upon the accuracy of his accounting, taking the experience as a corrective lesson.

parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys attends the Committee of Tangier where the Lord Treasurer promises £15,000, which he notes will be short. He dines with Creed and encounters a boastful would-be poet, then receives his wife's brother and promises to help find him a living. He walks to Woolwich and agrees it will be a good place for his wife and himself to spend the summer. Returning weary, he works until midnight and notes the plague increasing mightily, having seen a house shut up in the street, which he calls a sad sight.

parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys travels to White Hall and finds the Court full of wagons and people leaving town. He meets Mary at the Harp and Ball but stops conversing upon learning she lived at his neighbour's house. He notes the plague mortality bill has risen to 267, though only four deaths are in the City, which he calls a great blessing. He conducts business with Creed and takes leave of Mr. Coventry, observes the Queen-Mother departing for France, then returns home to dine merrily with Mrs. Hunt and work at his office, resolving to try working by daylight for a month.
parsed.narrative.meaning: The plague's toll, while rising overall, spares the City for now, which Pepys regards as a great blessing.

parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys woke worried about a mysterious letter but his wife reassured him it likely came from her cousin Franke Moore, and he chose to let the matter pass. He spent the morning resolving the shipwrights' desertion from work due to unpaid wages, and hosted Lord Bruncker and others at a modest dinner. In the evening, a dispute over a transcribed book of Rates ended with its cancellation, causing rancour in the woman involved. Throughout the day he was in great trouble over his boy Tom, who had gone to Greenwich and not returned for fear of the plague, though Tom came home safely that night.
parsed.narrative.meaning: He concluded the letter could not have much in it and chose not to vex himself while otherwise at ease.

parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys resolved a minor dispute with his wife over a letter, then spent the morning with Lord Bruncker investigating the shipwrights' desertion from work due to unpaid wages, bringing it to a hopeful resolution. At dinner and through the afternoon he entertained guests, and later oversaw the reluctant cancellation of a finely transcribed book of Rates, which vexed its owner. He walked in the fields with his wife in the evening, and was in great trouble all day for his boy Tom, who had gone to Greenwich and not returned until nightfall for fear of the plague.
parsed.narrative.meaning: It is better not to vex oneself over uncertain matters when one is otherwise at ease, especially in a strange place at a melancholy time.

Batten's. They played billiards, joked about a warrant for deer that vexed Sir W. Hickes, and agreed to dine with him again only to annoy him for being niggardly. On returning, he dealt curtly with Lord Rutherford's demands for Tangier money, then went to Woolwich to play backgammon with his wife.

He dines with his wife, takes leave of her, and works until past one in the morning.
